blocks.text: 美国政府已下令所有联邦文职机构从其计算机中移除 DeepSeek，并停止采购该产品，以及任何基于这家中国实验室 AI 构建的第三方产品。国土安全部于周一依据 2018 年的一项供应链法律，向《联邦公报》提交了该命令的通知，该法律允许其将高风险技术排除在政府系统之外。

blocks.text: DeepSeek 禁令涵盖的范围

inlines.text: DeepSeek 禁令涵盖的范围

blocks.text: 该命令要求所有文职机构做两件事。第一，将杭州深度求索人工智能及其关联公司和产品排除在采购之外，“立即生效”，包括机构批准的产品清单、电子商务市场和类似采购渠道。第二，立即从机构 IT 系统中移除 DeepSeek 及其关联公司的产品，“以及使用 DeepSeek 实现方案开发的第三方产品和服务”。

inlines.text: 该命令要求所有文职机构做两件事。第一，将杭州深度求索人工智能及其关联公司和产品排除在采购之外，“立即生效”，包括机构批准的产品清单、电子商务市场和类似采购渠道。第二，立即从机构 IT 系统中移除 DeepSeek 及其关联公司的产品，“以及使用 DeepSeek 实现方案开发的第三方产品和服务”。

blocks.text: 第二项条款范围很广。DeepSeek 的模型以开放权重形式发布，因此它们不仅出现在 DeepSeek 自己的应用和网站中，也出现在其他公司的工具里。该命令没有列出具体涉及哪些产品，也没有说明各机构应如何对待运行在美国公司服务器上的 DeepSeek 模型。该命令出台的几天前，DeepSeek 更新了其廉价的 Flash 模型，并称该模型目前在某些编程任务上已胜过 Claude Opus 5。

blocks.text: “多重威胁载体”：国土安全部为何称 DeepSeek 存在风险

inlines.text: “多重威胁载体”：国土安全部为何称 DeepSeek 存在风险

blocks.text: 该命令的风险摘要称，DeepSeek 的服务器位于中国，而中国法律“赋予政府网络和情报职能广泛权限，可访问私营公司基础设施”。命令称，DeepSeek 的注册流程会收集个人信息，并可能“追踪用户并对用户进行数字指纹识别”，其应用依赖用户输入信息来运作，这可能意味着美国政府工作人员或承包商的敏感数据最终流入中国。

blocks.text: 该命令称，这些信息与公开数据结合后，“可能生成关于美国人员和/或政府项目的可付诸行动的情报”。命令还补充说，这些模型“可能包含恶意软件或其他安全漏洞”，并援引 2025 年 2 月 NowSecure 的审计结果，该审计发现 DeepSeek 的 iPhone 应用存在多个严重缺陷。

blocks.text: 例外情形与 60 天窗口期

inlines.text: 例外情形与 60 天窗口期

blocks.text: 无法合规的机构可以申请例外，例如让该命令不适用于自身、不适用于某些操作，或申请延期。申请必须在命令发布后60天内以书面形式提出，并附上“充分理由”，例如对关键任务工作的影响，以及任何替代性防护措施。网络安全和基础设施安全局（CISA）负责审查这些申请，并以书面形式批准或拒绝。

blocks.text: 在DeepSeek产品被清除之前，各机构被要求监控进出其网络的流量、加强日志记录、增加防止数据离开其系统的控制措施，并标记任何异常情况。CISA可以帮助缺乏合规能力的机构，部长必须在一年内审查该命令，此后每年审查一次。

blocks.text: 全球范围内的DeepSeek禁令

inlines.text: 全球范围内的DeepSeek禁令

blocks.text: 据路透社报道，美国政府的多个部门已在各自设备上封禁DeepSeek，包括商务部和海军，纽约州、田纳西州和弗吉尼亚州等州也是如此。在国外，意大利数据保护机构于2025年初封禁了DeepSeek应用，台湾、韩国和澳大利亚则禁止在政府设备上使用该应用。周一的命令更进一步，覆盖了所有文职机构及其采购的一切。

blocks.text: 为何重要

inlines.text: 为何重要

blocks.text: 这是美国政府迄今针对一家中国AI实验室的最广泛举措，而且由于该命令覆盖了基于DeepSeek构建的第三方工具，它把负担压给了每一家向联邦机构销售AI的供应商，要求它们知道自己产品中内置了哪些模型。中国的开源模型位居全球下载量最高之列，而很少有模型在发布时公布安全结果，因此预计会有更多买家开始提出同样的问题。

blocks.text: The US government has ordered every federal civilian agency to strip DeepSeek out of its computers and stop buying it, along with any third-party product built on the Chinese lab's AI. The Department of Homeland Security filed notice of the order with the Federal Register on Monday, under a 2018 supply chain law that lets it bar risky technology from government systems.

blocks.text: The order, numbered 2026-01 and signed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, is dated July 24, 2026. It was kept out of public view until this week. Its notice is due to appear in the Federal Register on Tuesday, October 20, under docket DHS-2026-0628.

blocks.text: What the DeepSeek ban covers

inlines.text: What the DeepSeek ban covers

blocks.text: The order tells all civilian agencies to do two things. First, exclude Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence, its affiliates and their products from purchasing "effective immediately", including agency-approved product lists, e-commerce marketplaces and similar buying channels. Second, remove products from DeepSeek and its affiliates, "and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations", from agency IT systems immediately.

inlines.text: The order tells all civilian agencies to do two things. First, exclude Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence, its affiliates and their products from purchasing "effective immediately", including agency-approved product lists, e-commerce marketplaces and similar buying channels. Second, remove products from DeepSeek and its affiliates, "and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations", from agency IT systems immediately.

blocks.text: That second clause is the wide one. DeepSeek's models are released as open weights, so they turn up inside other companies' tools as well as in DeepSeek's own app and website. The order does not list which products it means, and it does not say how agencies should treat a DeepSeek model running on a US company's servers. It also comes days after DeepSeek updated its cheap Flash model, which it says now beats Claude Opus 5 at some coding tasks.

blocks.text: It does not reach the military or spy agencies. The order applies to federal civilian executive branch agencies "except for their national security systems and secure compartmented information systems", which fall under the Pentagon and the Director of National Intelligence.

blocks.text: "Multiple threat vectors": why DHS says DeepSeek is a risk

inlines.text: "Multiple threat vectors": why DHS says DeepSeek is a risk

blocks.text: The order's summary of risks says DeepSeek's servers are in China and that Chinese law "permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure". It says DeepSeek's sign-up process collects personal information and may "track and digitally fingerprint users", and that its apps work by having people type in information, which could mean sensitive data from US government staff or contractors ends up in China.

It says DeepSeek's sign-up process collects personal information and may "track and digitally fingerprint users", and that its apps work by having people type in information, which could mean sensitive data from US government staff or contractors ends up in China.

blocks.text: Combined with public data, that information "could produce actionable intelligence on U.S. persons and/or government programs", the order says. It adds that the models "may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities", and cites a February 2025 NowSecure audit that found multiple critical flaws in DeepSeek's iPhone app.

blocks.text: Exceptions and the 60-day window

inlines.text: Exceptions and the 60-day window

blocks.text: Agencies that can't comply can ask for an exception, such as having the order not apply to them, to certain actions, or a delay. Requests must be made in writing within 60 days of the order's issue, with a "compelling justification", for example the impact on mission-critical work, and any alternative safeguards. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) reviews them and approves or refuses in writing.

Requests must be made in writing within 60 days of the order's issue, with a "compelling justification", for example the impact on mission-critical work, and any alternative safeguards. blocks.text: Until DeepSeek products are gone, agencies are told to monitor traffic in and out of their networks, step up logging, add controls against data leaving their systems and flag anything unusual. CISA can help agencies that lack the skills to comply, and the Secretary must review the order within a year and every year after.

blocks.text: DeepSeek bans around the world

inlines.text: DeepSeek bans around the world

blocks.text: Several parts of the US government already blocked DeepSeek on their own devices, including the Commerce Department and the Navy, as did states including New York, Tennessee and Virginia, Reuters reported. Abroad, Italy's data protection authority blocked the DeepSeek app in early 2025, and Taiwan, South Korea and Australia barred it from government devices. Monday's order goes further, covering every civilian agency and everything they buy.

blocks.text: DeepSeek hasn't commented. The Chinese embassy in Washington didn't immediately comment, according to Reuters. The order lands as Beijing tightens its own grip on the sector: China now wants to control exports of its largest AI models, and DeepSeek is training its next model on Chinese chips.

blocks.text: Why it matters

inlines.text: Why it matters

blocks.text: This is the US government's broadest move yet against a Chinese AI lab, and by reaching third-party tools built on DeepSeek it puts the burden on every vendor selling AI to federal agencies to know which models sit inside their products. Chinese open models are among the most downloaded in the world, and few publish safety results at launch, so expect more buyers to start asking the same question.
